title: India Declares Indus Treaty 'Cannot Function,' Plans 5,500 MW of New J&K Hydro Projects
excerpt: New Delhi hardens its stance on the suspended water-sharing agreement with Pakistan, fast-tracking major dam projects on the Chenab and Jhelum rivers.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India declares the Indus Waters Treaty non-functional, escalating tensions with Pakistan.
  • Plans for 5,500 MW of new hydropower capacity in Jammu & Kashmir are underway.
  • Four major hydropower projects have fast-tracked commissioning dates to 2026-2028.
  • India rejects a ruling from an arbitration court, claiming it lacks legitimacy.
  • Pakistan warns that diverting treaty waters could be viewed as an 'act of war.'
  • India has declared the Indus Waters Treaty can no longer function in its current form, signaling a hardening of its stance more than a year after suspending the 1960 agreement.
  • New Delhi plans to build approximately 5,500 MW of new hydropower capacity in Jammu & Kashmir, with state-run NHPC leading development on the Chenab and Jhelum rivers.
  • Four major projects — the 1,000 MW Pakal Dul, 624 MW Kiru, 540 MW Kwar and 850 MW Ratle — have been fast-tracked, with commissioning dates advanced to between May 2026 and July 2028.
  • India has rejected a May 2026 ruling from what it calls an "illegally constituted" Court of Arbitration, while Pakistan has warned that diverting treaty waters would constitute an "act of war."

India has escalated its position on the suspended Indus Waters Treaty, declaring that the 66-year-old agreement with Pakistan can no longer function in its current form. The statement represents the most definitive language New Delhi has used since placing the treaty in abeyance in April 2025, following the Pahalgam terror attack in Kashmir that killed 26 people.

Accompanying the diplomatic shift is an ambitious infrastructure push. India now plans to add approximately 5,500 MW of new hydropower capacity in Jammu & Kashmir through a series of large dam and run-of-river projects on the Chenab and Jhelum rivers — waterways the treaty had largely designated for Pakistan's use.

Projects Gain Momentum

Four hydropower projects already under construction have been fast-tracked since the treaty's suspension. The 1,000 MW Pakal Dul on the Marusudar river (a Chenab tributary), the 624 MW Kiru, the 540 MW Kwar and the 850 MW Ratle — all on the Chenab — have had their commissioning schedules advanced by several months, according to officials familiar with the matter. The Ratle project is expected to be the first completed, with commissioning targeted for May 2026.

Beyond these, NHPC, India's largest hydropower company, has floated a tender for the long-delayed 1,856 MW Sawalkot project on the Chenab, one of the biggest planned dams in the region. Work has also begun on Dulhasti Stage II (260 MW) and Uri-I Stage 2 (240 MW), with construction starting in recent months.

India has additionally announced plans for a Dahi Nallah diversion project that would redirect water from a Chenab tributary through a tunnel to the existing 330 MW Kishanganga project, adding an estimated 30 million units of electricity annually.

Breaking Free of Treaty Constraints

The Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank and signed in 1960 by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru and Pakistan's General Ayub Khan, divided the six rivers of the Indus system between the two nations. India received the three eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — while Pakistan received the three western rivers: Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, with India permitted only limited, non-consumptive use.

The treaty capped India's storage capacity on the western rivers at 3.6 million acre feet (MAF). With the treaty now in abeyance, India can pursue reservoir projects and conduct regular de-silting operations that were previously restricted. The average annual runoff of the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab is estimated at 136 MAF, of which approximately 40% — around 54 MAF — originates from the Indian side.

"With the Indus Water Treaty in abeyance, India would now be able to take up projects which have been planned for a long time but Pakistan has objected to."

— Former NHPC Chairman, speaking to Livemint

India has identified a total potential hydropower capacity of 18,217 MW on the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab rivers, with the Chenab alone accounting for 14,000 MW. Operational projects currently total over 3.3 GW, with another 2.56 GW under construction and detailed project reports prepared for an additional 12.25 GW.

Diplomatic Tensions Deepen

Pakistan has strongly opposed India's moves, with officials warning that any diversion of treaty-designated waters would be considered an "act of war." Islamabad has also sought international support, including approaching Canada for diplomatic assistance in reviving the agreement.

India has rejected a May 15, 2026, ruling from what it describes as an "illegally constituted" Court of Arbitration regarding treaty interpretation and maximum pondage, asserting it does not recognize the court's authority. The Ministry of External Affairs has maintained that the treaty's restoration is contingent on Pakistan "credibly and irreversibly" ending its support for cross-border terrorism.

What It Means for the Diaspora

Impact of the Indus Waters Treaty
›Treaty signed in 1960, dividing river usage between India and Pakistan.
›India's storage capacity on western rivers capped at 3.6 million acre feet.
›Average annual runoff of Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab: 136 MAF.
›40% of runoff (54 MAF) originates from Indian territory.

For the Indian diaspora, particularly those with roots in Jammu & Kashmir, the hydropower push carries significant implications. The region's development has long been constrained by treaty restrictions, with a 2005 study estimating that the agreement cost J&K approximately ₹6,500 crore annually in foregone agricultural and hydropower potential. The new projects promise economic development and employment in a region that has historically lagged, though construction timelines spanning into 2028 and beyond mean tangible benefits remain years away.

The stakes extend beyond energy. India's control over water infrastructure on the western rivers gives it leverage in one of the world's most consequential transboundary water disputes, with implications for food security, regional stability and the future of India-Pakistan relations.
